The ancient poets usually give horns to Bacchus. It is therefore quite wonderful, says Spence, that one so rarely catches sight of these horns on his statues. <margin>a) <term>Polymetis</term> <gloss>a work by Joseph Spence</gloss> Dialogue IX. page 129.</margin> <note>a</note> He hits upon this cause, then another: on the ignorance of antiquarians, or on the smallness of the horns themselves, which might have hidden themselves beneath the grapes and ivy leaves, the constant head-dress of the god. He winds himself around the true cause without suspecting it. The horns of Bacchus were not natural horns, as they were on the fauns and satyrs. They were a forehead-ornament which he could put on and take off.

> To you, when you stand without horns,
> belongs a maidenly head: — —
> <note>original Latin: "Tibi, cum sine cornibus adstas / Virgineum caput est:" from Ovid's Metamorphoses.</note>

<note>a) Joseph Spence (1699–1768) was an English historian and literary figure whose work Polymetis compared Roman poetry and ancient art.</note>

<summary>Lessing criticizes Joseph Spence for failing to recognize that poetry has a wider range of expression than painting, specifically regarding the depiction of Bacchus with horns.</summary>

for some hours still, as we say, whitish, finally after the fourth or sixth day, they deposit everything, remaining pure and clear: can their resistance to penetration stop those impalpable and insensible atoms of sand <note>original: "atomi di rena"</note> which, due to their very minimal force, take six days to descend the space of half a cubit? What then is this thickness of the water with which it resists division? What, in our faith, shall it be, if we (even as I have also said above) with every diligence trying to reduce a material so similar in gravity to water that, by forming it even into a very wide sheet, it remains suspended, as we say, between the two waters; it is impossible to achieve it, although we bring ourselves to such a similarity of equal weight <note>original: "equiponderanza"</note> that as much lead as is the fourth part of a grain of millet, added to the said very wide sheet, which in air would weigh four or six pounds, leads it to the bottom, and when removed, it comes to the surface of the water? I cannot see (if what I say is true, as it is most true) what minimum virtue and force could be found or imagined, of which the reluctance of the water <note>original: "renitenza dell'acqua"</note> to being divided and pulled apart is not smaller, from which, by necessity, it is concluded that it is nothing: because if it were of some sensible power, some wide sheet could be found or composed of material similar in gravity to water, which would not only stop between the two waters, but could not be lowered or raised without notable force. 

We could likewise gather the same truth from another experiment, showing how the water in the same way yields also to transverse division, because if in still and stagnant water we place any very large mass that does not go to the bottom, pulling it with a single hair from a woman's head, we will lead it from place to place without any opposition, even if its shape be whatever one wishes, such that it embraces a great space of water, as a large beam moved crosswise would do. Perhaps someone might oppose me, saying that if the resistance of water to being divided were, as I affirm, nothing, ships should not need such force of oars or sails to be pushed from place to place in the calm sea or in stagnant lakes. To whoever made such oppositions I would answer that water does not contrast or resist simply being divided, but indeed being divided quickly, and with much greater reluctance as the velocity <note>original: "velocità"</note> is greater: and the cause of such resistance does not depend on thickness or anything else that absolutely opposes division, but

<summary>Galileo argues that water has zero internal resistance or tenacity because even minute particles of sand eventually sink through it. He demonstrates that huge objects can be moved through water with minimal force, concluding that water only resists rapid movement, not division itself.</summary>
<keywords>viscosity, density, resistance, division, velocity, buoyancy, experiment</keywords>

And the fruition-giving inclination of the spirit, which seeks rest in God above all likeness, obtains and possesses supernaturally in its essential being all that the spirit ever received naturally therein. All good people have this, but how it is remains hidden from them all their lives, unless they are inward and empty of all creatures and enlightened with spiritual understanding. In the same <margin>As soon as a person turns from sins, he is received by God.</margin> moment that a person turns away from sins, he is received by God into the essential unity of himself, in the highest part of his spirit, so that he may rest in God now and always. And he receives grace and a likeness to God in the property of his powers, so that he may always grow and increase in virtues. And as long as that likeness persists in <term>charity</term> <gloss>divine love</gloss> and in virtues, so does the unity persist in rest; and it cannot be lost except through mortal sin.

<summary>This page explains that the soul receives the entire Trinity and the divine nature when united with God. Ruusbroec emphasizes that this unity is established the moment a person turns from sin and is only lost through mortal sin.</summary>
<keywords>Holy Spirit, Trinity, divine nature, essential unity, charity, mortal sin, Ruusbroec, spiritual understanding</keywords>

I say then that in the first method, which is that <term>festiua narratione</term> <gloss>festive narration</gloss>, there is no need for any art; for nature itself creates and forms men capable of narrating pleasantly, and gives them the face, gestures, voice, and words appropriate for imitating whatever they wish. In the other method, that of witticisms, what can art do? Since that salty saying must have come out and hit the mark before it appears that the one who says it could have thought of it; otherwise it is cold and lacks excellence. Therefore I believe that the whole matter is the work of talent and nature.

Then Messer <note>original: "M."</note> Pietro Bembo <note>A celebrated Venetian scholar and later Cardinal, influential in the development of the Italian language.</note> replied and said, "The Lord Prefect <note>Francesco Maria della Rovere, the Duke of Urbino and Prefect of Rome.</note> does not deny what you say, which is that nature and talent hold the primary roles, especially regarding <term>inuentione</term> <gloss>invention or the finding of ideas</gloss>. But it is certain that in the mind of everyone, no matter how good their talent may be, there are born good and bad concepts, more or less; but judgment thereafter and art refine and correct them, making a selection of the good and rejecting the bad. Therefore, leaving aside what belongs to talent, explain to us what consists in art—namely, the <term>facetie</term> <gloss>jests</gloss> and the <term>motti</term> <gloss>witticisms</gloss> that induce laughter. Tell us which are suitable for the Courtier and which are not, and in what time and manner they should be used, for this is what the Lord Prefect asks of you."

Then Messer Federico, still laughing, said, "There is no one here among us to whom I do not yield in everything, and especially in being witty—unless perhaps the foolish things that often make others laugh more than fine sayings were also accepted as jests." And so turning to Count Ludovico <note>Ludovico di Canossa, a diplomat and relative of Castiglione.</note> and to Messer Bernardo Bibiena <note>Bernardo Dovizi da Bibiena, a playwright and diplomat known for his sharp wit.</note>, he said, "Here are the masters of this."

<summary>Federico Fregoso argues that wit is a natural talent rather than a learned art, while Pietro Bembo suggests that judgment and art are needed to refine natural ideas. Federico then points to Ludovico di Canossa and Bernardo Bibiena as the true experts in humor.</summary>
<keywords>witticisms, nature vs art, Pietro Bembo, Federico Fregoso, Bernardo Bibiena, Ludovico di Canossa, judgment, courtly manners</keywords>

### CHAPTER LXVI.

**How the next day we sent messengers to the <term>Caciques</term> <gloss>tribal lords</gloss> of Tlascala, entreating them for peace, and what they did regarding this.**

After the battle I have described had passed, in which we captured the three principal Indians, our Captain Cortés sent them immediately, along with the two who were in our camp and had gone other times as messengers. He ordered them to tell the <term>Caciques</term> of Tlascala that we begged them to come in peace at once, and to give us passage through their land to go to Mexico, as we have sent to tell them other times. And if they do not come now, we will kill all their people; and because we love them much and wish to have them as brothers, we would not want to anger them if they had not given cause for it. Many flattering things were said to them to draw them to our friendship. Those messengers went willingly then to the capital of Tlascala and delivered their embassy to all the <term>Caciques</term> already named by me. They found them together with many other elders and <term>Papas</term> <gloss>priests</gloss>, and they were very sad, both because of the ill success of the war and the death of the captains, relatives, or sons of theirs who died in the battles. It is said they did not want to listen to them willingly; and what they agreed upon regarding this was that they immediately ordered all the diviners and <term>Papas</term> to be called, and others who cast lots, whom they call <term>Tacalnagual</term> <gloss>sorcerers/shape-shifters</gloss>, who are like wizards. They told them to look through their divinations, spells, and lots to see what kind of people we were, and if we could be defeated by giving us war day and night continually; and also to know if we were <term>Teules</term> <gloss>gods/demons</gloss>, just as the people of Cempoal said (as I have said other times, they are evil things like demons), and what things we ate, and to look into all this with great diligence. 

<margin>What the Indian diviners and their wizards said about our men.</margin>

After the diviners and wizards and many <term>Papas</term> gathered, and their divinations were performed, and their lots cast, and all that they were accustomed to do, it appears they said that in the lots they found we were men of bone and flesh, and that we ate chickens, and dogs, and bread, and fruit when we had it, and that we did not eat the flesh of Indians nor the hearts of those we killed. Because, as it appeared, the friendly Indians we brought from Cempoal had made them believe we were <term>Teules</term>, and that we ate the hearts of Indians, and that the <term>bombardas</term> <gloss>small cannons</gloss> threw lightning bolts as they fall from the sky, and that the <term>lebrel</term> <gloss>greyhound</gloss> was a tiger or lion, and that the horses were for spearing the Indians when we wanted to kill them; and they told them many other childish things. 

<margin>The Indian diviners make them believe that our men had no strength at night.</margin>

And let us return to the <term>Papas</term>; and the worst of all that their <term>Papas</term> and diviners told them was that by day we could not be defeated, but only by night, because as it grew dark our strength was taken from us. And the wizards told them more: that we were courageous, and that we had all these virtues by day until the sun set, and once it grew dark we had no strength at all. When the <term>Caciques</term> heard that and held it to be very certain, they sent to tell it to their General Captain Xicotenga, so that he would come quickly one night with great powers to give us war. When he knew this, he gathered about ten thousand of the most courageous Indians he had and came to our camp. From three sides they began to give us a hand of arrows, and to throw spears with their <term>tiraderas</term> <gloss>spear-throwers</gloss> of one barb and of two, and those with swords and <term>macanas</term> <gloss>obsidian-edged clubs</gloss> and two-handed swords from another side, in such a way that they suddenly held it for certain that they would carry some of us off to sacrifice. But our Lord God provided better; for as secretly as they came, they found us very prepared. Because as our scouts and spies felt the great noise they made while coming at breakneck speed, they came to give the alarm. And as we were so accustomed to sleeping with our boots on, and our armor worn, and the horses saddled and bridled, and all kinds of weapons ready, we resisted them with the muskets and crossbows, and with thrusts of the sword they quickly turned their backs. # Description of Lima, the City of Kings.

<margin>
Appearance of the city of Lima.
</margin>
In this city are good houses, some of which are very beautiful with small towers and galleries. The market square is large, and the streets are wide, all leading straight to the market, from where one may also see into every corner, and on both sides the open fields. Through the majority of the houses run channels which bring fresh water from the river, providing great convenience and comfort for the citizens; by this means they can water all their orchards and herb gardens, which they keep beautiful and pleasant. Also,

<margin>
Many watermills with which they grind their corn.
</margin>
in this river lie many watermills after the manner of our own land, where they grind their corn. In short, here live very wealthy citizens, some of whom possess 150,000 <term>ducats</term> <gloss>gold coins</gloss>. From this city, ships sometimes depart carrying a value of 800,000 ducats, and some even a million. On the east side, above the city, is a high mountain upon which stands a Crucifix. On another side outside the city, the citizens have their dwellings and places where they keep their livestock, as well as their dovecotes and vineyards—though the grapes are not good due to the nature of the soil—and beautiful gardens, filled not only with all kinds of fruits of that land: but also

<margin>
Description of the fertility of the land.
</margin>
those of Spain, such as figs, pomegranates, limes, lemons, oranges, melons, beans, peas, and sugar canes, all very tasty, indeed better than in Spain. Truly, to pass human life with joy—were it not for the scandalous disagreements and wars—this place is surely one of the most beautiful in the entire world. For the landscape there is so temperate that throughout the entire year there is no excessive heat or harmful cold; likewise, it has never been seen that hunger or plague occurred there, nor any rain, nor claps of thunder, nor lightning from Heaven

<margin>
Why the City of Kings obtained its name, and was built in the year 1535.
</margin>
striking. But on the contrary, there is always a clear, bright, and beautiful sky. It was founded by the Admiral Don Francisco Pizarro in the year 1535 and is named the City of the Kings because the people were brought into it on Epiphany <note>Three Kings Day</note>. Regarding provisions, besides the fish which they have in great abundance from the sea and river, as also meat and fruits of the trees and the earth as mentioned, there is no less abundance of wheat and grain. During the four months when it is summer in Spain, it is winter there, being a little colder than at other times. In these four winter months, a small dew or mist like a fog falls every day before noon, yet it is not unhealthy like ours; those who have pain in the head find relief by washing themselves with it. It is very apparent that this city of Lima shall daily increase in people and wealth, although many years ago there were already over 500 houses

<margin>
The width and length of the houses of Lima.
</margin>
there, and the city is built very spaciously so that 2000 might well stand there. For the streets are wide and the market square large; each house has a plot of 80 feet in width and 160 feet in length. And because there is no suitable wood to make upper floors—for within two or three years it is eaten away by worms—the houses are built with only one story, yet very

<margin>
Appearance of the houses.
</margin>
costly and magnificent with many chambers, halls, and parlors, fit to live in and to harbor foreign guests. The walls are made of certain materials which they bake together very thick and fill with earth. They roof their houses with painted mats or painted linen; all around and above

<column-break/>

on the walls, they make small bowers of greenery where they shelter from the sun. They do not need to worry about rain, for it does not rain there. This city has under its jurisdiction all these cities where Bishops reside: Quito, Cusco, Guamanga, Arequipa, Pax, Plata, Trujillo, Guanuco, Chachapoyas, Portus Vetus, Guayaquil, Popayan, Carchi, San Miguel, and San Francisco. It was said previously that Peru is divided into three kinds of landscapes: the flat land by the sea, the mountains or mountainous land running through the middle of Peru, and the land beyond the mountains. Of the flat land on the shore of the sea we have dealt until now, beginning from the Equator and Cape Passao to this point. It should further be known that from Tumbes not only to Lima, but much further south, the sea coast is very dry and full of large, desolate sandy places, where for ten miles inland there is no thunder, lightning, or rain; but beyond those ten miles—or however many miles more or less the mountains lie from the sea—it does rain. There are also no springs or wells in this flat land, but only four or five standing waters which are brackish because they lie near the sea. The inhabitants support themselves with water from the rivers that come from the mountains, which take their origin from the snow and rain that fall in the mountains, and not from springs, which are few in the mountains. The distances of these rivers were partly described before, lying 7, 8, 10, 12, 15, and 20 miles from one another, though mostly 7 or 8, by which traveling people regulate their journey, as they find no other water elsewhere. On both sides of these rivers, for a mile’s breadth or even wider, sometimes more, sometimes less, depending on the situation of the land, there are various fertile trees and corn lands which are cultivated and sown by the people, which they may do throughout the entire year. Also, many kinds of wild trees grow near these rivers: cotton, reeds, thistles, rushes, and irises, etc. And since the Spaniards have taken the land, they also sow wheat, making the land moist through certain channels which they lead out of these rivers. Because these rivers run swiftly down from high mountains, one can hardly cross them without help, and many have drowned therein. Those who make their journey along the flat land generally keep so close to the seaside that they always have it in sight. When it is winter in the mountains and rains heavily, it is dangerous to travel there because of the rising of the rivers that one must pass, either with certain rafts they have for that purpose, or with a net which they fill tightly with gourds, upon which the traveling man must lie stretched out; one of the Indians swims in front, pulling that net or raft forward with a cord, and another steers from behind. The people of the flat land live in huts made of greenery. The men wear shirts and cloths reaching to the knees and extending beyond, and an upper garment like a cloak. The women wear a coarse garment of cotton according to the length of the body; and although the fashion of the clothing is almost the same everywhere, there is nonetheless some distinction in the decoration of the head: for some wear single small cords, some braided, some of one color, others of various colors; and there is no one who does not wear something on the head, all distinguished according to the custom of the land.
